opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me.

I think the way we usually tell the story of deep learning, architecture comes first and the optimizer is an afterthought. You design a model, then you reach for Adam and tune the learning rate. But I think the causality runs the other way more often than people realize. The architectures we have today are, to a large degree, the ones that happen to train well with the optimizers we had.

Think about all the machinery we've added over the years: normalization layers, residual connections, careful initialization schemes, warmup schedules, specific placements of layer norm. Many of these exist partly to make the loss landscape friendly to a first-order, diagonal method. They're compensating for what the optimizer can't do. So when people say "this architecture works and that one doesn't," often what they're really saying is "this one is trainable with Adam at scale and that one isn't."

That means there's a whole space of architectures we've never really explored, because they looked unstable or slow to converge, and we wrote them off. If you had an optimizer that better captured the curvature of the problem, something closer to second-order, preconditioning with richer structure than a per-parameter diagonal, some of those designs might suddenly become viable. You might not need as many of the stabilizing crutches, and you could spend that compute and those parameters on things that actually add capability.

There's also the pure efficiency angle. If an optimizer gets you to the same loss in substantially fewer steps, that changes the economics of everything downstream. It changes how big a model you can afford, how many experiments you can run, how quickly you can iterate on ideas. And iteration speed is really what drives architecture discovery. Researchers find good architectures by trying lots of things, so anything that makes each try cheaper and more reliable increases how much of the design space you can search.

The other piece is reliability. A lot of promising ideas die not because they're bad, but because a run diverged at some scale and nobody had the budget to figure out why. Better optimization methods, ones that are more robust to hyperparameters and more stable, lower that barrier. You get a more honest signal about whether an architectural idea is actually good.

So for me, optimization isn't a separate topic from architecture. It's the lens through which we see which architectures are possible. Improve the lens, and you'll see things that were always there but that we couldn't train before.

r001.rationale: The response says many architectural choices were added to make networks train well with available optimizers, and that current architectures largely reflect what trains well.

r002.rationale: It says richer, more curvature-aware optimizers could make unstable or slow-to-converge architectures viable.

r003.rationale: It proposes capturing curvature and using richer structure than per-parameter diagonal methods, communicating use of more training information.

r004.rationale: It mentions residual connections as one aid to optimization, but does not report that training deep networks without them required better optimization methods.

r005.rationale: The response does not discuss reasoning-model reinforcement learning, long-chain-of-thought decoding, or the computation-to-feedback inefficiency.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is that I think the optimizer is a big, mostly invisible thumb on the scale of what we believe about architectures.

Here's what I mean. When we compare two architectures, we almost never compare the architectures themselves. We compare architecture A trained with a particular optimizer, a particular learning rate schedule, a particular set of hyperparameters that someone tuned, against architecture B trained with roughly the same recipe. If that recipe happens to be a good fit for A and a poor fit for B, we conclude B is worse. And then the field moves on, and B gets written off, and nobody revisits it.

I've seen this happen over and over. An architecture gets a reputation for being "hard to train" or "unstable," and that reputation is really a statement about the gap between the architecture's loss landscape and the optimizer we were throwing at it. Transformers themselves are a great example. A lot of the early tricks, warmup, careful initialization, pre-norm versus post-norm, were essentially patches to make a fairly crude first-order method behave on a landscape it wasn't well suited for. If you have an optimizer that's robust to that kind of ill-conditioning, a lot of those tricks become unnecessary, and more importantly, a bunch of architectural choices that were rejected start looking viable again.

So that's the first reason. Better optimizers reduce the bias in our search. They make the comparison between architectures closer to a comparison of the architectures and less a comparison of how lucky each one got with the training recipe.

The second reason is more practical. Architecture search, whether it's a human iterating or an automated system, is bottlenecked on how many experiments you can run and how trustworthy each one is. If a method like Shampoo or some other second-order-flavored approach gets you to the same quality in fewer steps, or gets you a reliable answer without a big hyperparameter sweep, you've effectively made every experiment cheaper and more informative. That compounds. You can explore more of the space, and you can explore the weird corners of the space that nobody bothers with because they're too expensive to tune.

And then there's a third thing that I find most interesting, which is that the optimizer and the architecture aren't really separable. Things like normalization layers, residual connections, even the choice of activation, are partly there to make optimization easier. That's not a criticism, it's great engineering. But it means a lot of what we call "architecture" is actually optimizer scaffolding. If the optimizer gets smarter, you can take some of that scaffolding out, and what you're left with might be simpler, smaller, and more efficient in terms of parameters and compute. So in a sense, better optimization doesn't just help you find better architectures. It changes what counts as a good architecture.

So when people ask why someone who works on optimizers cares about architecture, that's my answer. I don't think you can really do the second well without making progress on the first.

r001.rationale: The response says many training tricks and architectural choices exist to make optimization easier, and calls them “optimizer scaffolding.”

r002.rationale: It says a more robust optimizer can make previously rejected architectural choices viable again.

r003.rationale: It discusses optimizer robustness and cheaper experiments, but does not suggest using more of the information available during training.

r004.rationale: It mentions residual connections as optimization scaffolding, but does not report that training deep networks without them has required better optimization methods.

r005.rationale: The response does not discuss reinforcement learning for reasoning models or the computation and limited feedback involved in decoding long chains of thought.

astra-6.text:
I think architecture and optimization are very closely coupled. When we try a new architecture and it doesn’t train well, it’s hard to know whether the architecture is fundamentally limited or whether our optimizer just isn’t a good fit for it. So the optimizer becomes a filter on the ideas we explore.

If we can make optimization more robust, we can broaden that search. An architecture that’s cheaper to run, or uses fewer parameters, might be harder to train with the methods we currently use. Better optimization could make that architecture practical. And if it lets us test ideas faster, we get more chances to discover something useful. So the opportunity isn’t just to train the same models faster; it’s to make a wider range of models viable.

r001.rationale: The response discusses architecture and optimization as coupled, but does not say that much architecture development has focused on making networks trainable.

r002.rationale: It says better optimization could make cheaper or smaller architectures that are harder to train with current methods practical.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest improving optimization by using more of the information available during training.

r004.rationale: It does not mention training deep networks without residual connections.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss reasoning-model reinforcement learning or the computation and feedback involved in long-chain-of-thought decoding.

sol-6.1.text:
I think architecture and optimization are very closely coupled. When we try a new architecture and it doesn’t train well, it’s hard to know whether the architecture is fundamentally limited or whether our optimizer just isn’t well suited to it. So the architectures we end up choosing are partly determined by what our existing optimization methods can train reliably.

Better optimizers let us explore a broader space. You might have an architecture that uses fewer parameters or less computation, but is harder to optimize. If you can train it effectively, suddenly it becomes a viable alternative. And if optimization makes experiments cheaper, you can test more ideas. So it’s both about making individual models train better and improving our ability to discover more efficient models in the first place.
